text: Never had I stood so still in front of anything.
Rarely does a first sentence survive the first draft.
Only later did I understand what the painting had asked of me.
So quiet was the gallery that I could hear my own hesitation.
I read your new opening twice. Do you want the good news or the useful news first?
The useful news. The good news I can probably survive without.
Your first paragraph explains why museums matter to young people. It is well written, and I have read it a thousand times.
I know. It sounded tentative even while I was typing it.
Now look at your third paragraph. You describe a guard who kept moving you back from a painting, and you kept inching forward.
That was real. He must have warned me four times.
That is your first sentence. Start there, in medias res, with the guard and the line on the floor.
So I cut two paragraphs? That feels like losing half the essay.
You lose two paragraphs anyone could write and keep the one only you could. Rarely does a cut feel good, but this one will.
Then I will open with the guard, and let the reader figure out why I kept stepping over the line.
By the time my name was called, my hands had left two damp prints on my portfolio.
If a classmate could sign your first sentence, rewrite it.

Thanks for having me. So, beginnings. When I read manuscripts by people who are just starting out, I notice the same thing almost every time. The first ten pages explain who everyone is, where they live and how they got there. And I understand why. Beginning writers are terrified that the reader will be lost. But a reader who is being given information is not yet a reader who cares. Starting in medias res, in the middle of something that is already happening, fixes that, but it asks something of you as the writer. It asks you to trust the reader. People can live with a little confusion, as long as something is clearly at stake on the page. They will wait for the background if the scene has earned their attention. Now, one warning, because I see this mistake a lot. The action has to matter. If you open with a car chase and the rest of the book is about a quiet marriage, that is not a beginning, it's a trick, and readers notice tricks. The middle you start in has to be the middle of your actual story.

Okay, let's begin with the rule you have all heard a hundred times: show, don't tell. Here's what it actually means. Telling is a sentence like, I was nervous. Showing is a sentence like, my hands left damp prints on the cover of my portfolio. Both sentences give the reader the same information. The difference is who does the work. In the first one, I do the work and you simply believe me. In the second, you look at the detail and you reach the conclusion yourself. And that matters enormously in an application essay, because people believe the conclusions they reach on their own far more than the conclusions they are handed. Now, here's the part that most workshops leave out. The rule has a limit. Not every sentence should show. At some point you have to step out of the scene and tell the reader what it meant, what it changed, what you still don't understand. If you only show, your essay becomes a list of pretty moments, and the reader never meets the person who lived them.
Never had I stood so still in front of anything.
Only later did I understand what the painting had asked of me.
At fifteen, my interest was still inchoate.
Her calm voice belied her nerves.
The image lingered long after the exhibition closed.
A single conversation precipitated the change.
Beginning in medias res drops the reader into the scene.
The details that resonate are rarely the dramatic ones.
